name: diagnose-slow-machine
description: The machine is slow, swapping, or close to falling over: find which resource is running out, who holds it, and what to do.
template:
This machine is slow or unstable. Diagnose it with hearth's tools, in this order, and stop as soon as the cause is clear:

1. Call `doctor` with watch_seconds 30. Note memory pressure, available memory, swap, and any open-file, thread or CLOSE_WAIT growth with its projected time to the limit.
2. Call `diff` with kind "doctor" and from "~10" to see what moved across recent recorded observations; steady growth in one process across snapshots is a leak. If there are not enough snapshots, step 1 has just recorded one: say that history starts now and go on.
3. Call `incidents` with since set to today's date to see whether the kernel already panicked, killed (jetsam or OOM) or found hung tasks.
4. Call `ports` with runtimes_only true to see which model servers are resident and how much memory each holds.

Then answer in this shape: the resource that is running out; the process responsible, with evidence from the tools; what to do now, naming the exact server or process; and what to watch for. Do not stop or restart anything yourself unless it is a server hearthd owns (see `status`) and the user asked for it.

name: server-died
description: A model server stopped answering, crashed, or keeps failing requests: find out why and whether hearth already recovered it.

arguments.name: server
arguments.description: Name in hearthd's [servers], or the port the server listens on.

template:
A model server stopped working (named: {server}; if unknown, find the failing one in the steps below). Find out why:

1. Call `status` to see whether hearthd owns it: its state (ready, waiting, gave_up), restart count and last event. If hearthd is not running, say so and continue.
2. If hearthd owns it, call `logs` with that server for its last output: a load error, a missing file, an out-of-memory line. Then call `log` with kind "run" and limit 30. Read the events for this server in order: exited (with code or signal), wedged (stopped answering), poisoned (backend latched after an out-of-memory error; it answers /health but fails every request), not_ready, give_up.
3. Call `ports` to see what answers on its port now, and whether it is reported as not answering.
4. Call `incidents` with since set to today's date: a jetsam or OOM kill of this process explains an exit with signal 9.
5. Call `diff` with kind "ports" to see when it vanished or restarted.

Answer with: the cause (exit, wedge, poisoned backend, killed for memory, or crash loop), the evidence, and the fix. If hearthd owns it and is no longer restarting it, offer `restart` and say what will happen. If memory was the cause, say which other servers to unload first (from `ports`) and suggest a smaller context, checked with `fit`.

name: can-i-load
description: Before starting a model server: will this model at this context fit the device, and right now, and what would have to go first?

arguments.name: model
arguments.description: Path to a .gguf file, or an Ollama model name such as qwen3:8b.

arguments.name: ctx
arguments.description: Total context tokens the server will allocate (llama.cpp -c; Ollama num_ctx x parallel).

arguments.name: cache_type
arguments.description: KV cache type, e.g. f16 or q8_0 (default f16).

template:
Decide whether {model} with {ctx} tokens of context can be loaded on this machine.

1. Call `fit` with model "{model}", ctx {ctx} and cache_type "{cache_type}". Note fits_device, fits_now, the largest context that would fit, and the notes (fits_now is provisional until the P0 gate has measured how memory-mapped weights count).
2. Call `doctor` to see memory pressure and available memory now.
3. Call `ports` with runtimes_only true to see which models are resident and their footprints.

Answer yes or no for the device and for right now. If it does not fit now, say which resident servers would have to be unloaded (largest first, from `ports`; hearthd's own can be unloaded with `stop` if the user agrees), or the largest context that fits. Never load or start the model yourself.

name: what-changed
description: What changed on this machine since an earlier observation: servers that appeared, vanished, restarted or went silent; memory and descriptor movement; supervision events. Compare with a tag (hearth tag healthy) to see what differs from a known good state.

arguments.name: since
arguments.description: How far back to compare: ~N for N snapshots back, @AGE for a time ago (@2h, @1d), or a tag name such as healthy (default ~1).

template:
Report what changed on this machine against {since} (~N is N snapshots back, @2h is two hours ago, a name is a tag). Call `tag` with no name to list tags.

1. Call `diff` with kind "ports" and from "{since}": model servers that appeared, vanished, restarted (new pid) or stopped answering, and footprint movement.
2. Call `diff` with kind "doctor" and from "{since}" and limit 10: memory pressure, available memory, swap, and the processes whose open files, threads or CLOSE_WAIT sockets moved most.
3. Call `log` with kind "run" and limit 20 for supervision events in that time.

If `diff` says there are not enough snapshots, call `ports` and `doctor` once to record a fresh one and say that history starts now. Summarize the changes that matter first: restarts, silences, pressure, growth toward a limit.

name: find-a-leak
description: Something is leaking open files, threads or sockets, or a server keeps growing: find which process, since when, and how fast.

arguments.name: suspect
arguments.description: Part of a process name or pid to follow, if one is suspected (default: find it first).

template:
Find a leak on this machine. Suspect: {suspect}.

1. Call `doctor` with watch_seconds 30; its trend names processes whose open files, threads or CLOSE_WAIT sockets are growing, with the time to their limit.
2. Call `diff` with kind "doctor", from "~10" and limit 10 to see which processes moved most across recorded observations.
3. For the process that stands out (or the suspect), call `follow` with that name and kind "doctor" to see its counts in every recorded snapshot: steady growth is a leak, a sawtooth is normal churn. If it is a model server, also `follow` it with kind "ports" for its footprint, and with kind "run" for restarts.

Answer with the process, the resource, the growth rate and since when, the projected time to its limit, and what to do (restart it before the limit; CLOSE_WAIT growth means a server not closing sockets after clients disconnect). If there is too little history, say so: hearth watch, or hearthd, records it from now on.

name: when-did-it-start
description: When something first showed up on this machine, and what changed just then: an error, a finding code, a model, a port or a pid, found in hearth's recorded history.

arguments.name: what
arguments.description: The text to look for: an error message, a finding code such as oversized or partial_offload, a model name, a port or a pid.

template:
Find when "{what}" first appeared in hearth's history, and what changed at that moment. Only read: do not load a model or restart anything.

1. Call `log` with grep "{what}" for each kind: "ports", "doctor" and "run". Each match has a back number N: it is snapshot ~N.
2. Take the oldest match of the kind that has one (its largest back number, N). If no snapshot of that kind is older (`log` with stats gives the count), it was there when the history starts: say so.
3. Otherwise call `diff` with that kind, from "~(N+1)" and to "~N": what changed between the last snapshot without it and the first with it. Call `show` with that kind and "~N" if the diff does not explain it.
4. If the matches stop before ~0, it went away: diff the newest match against the snapshot after it the same way.

Answer when it started (and ended, if it did), what changed at that moment, and what to do. If `log` has too few snapshots, say so: hearth watch, or hearthd, records from now on.
